concepts.name: IUCN Red List: Organizational Structure and Authority
key_dimensions: IUCN as a body — its hybrid nature (union of governments AND civil society, not a UN body)
Species Survival Commission (SSC) as the technical arm that conducts assessments
Non-binding nature of Red List listings vs. legally binding CITES appendices — a common UPSC trap
Difference between IUCN Red List of Threatened Species vs. IUCN Red List of Ecosystems

concepts.name: The Nine Red List Categories: Hierarchy and Logic
key_dimensions: Correct order: EX → EW → CR → EN → VU → NT → LC → DD → NE
Three 'threatened' categories (CR, EN, VU) vs. the broader set of nine — examinees often miscount
Categories that are NOT assessed: Not Evaluated (NE) — frequently confused with Data Deficient (DD)
The distinction between 'threatened' (CR/EN/VU) and 'near threatened' (NT) for trap-based MCQs

concepts.name: Extinct (EX) Category: Criteria and Confirmation
key_dimensions: Definition: No reasonable doubt that the last individual has died — 'exhaustive surveys' requirement
Time threshold considerations: surveys must cover known habitats, life cycle, time of day/season
Difference between EX and EW — species is EX only when extinct in both wild AND captivity
Indian examples: Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus venaticus declared EX in wild in India) vs. globally EX species like Pink-headed Duck

concepts.name: Extinct in the Wild (EW) Category: Conservation Paradox
key_dimensions: Survives only in cultivation, captivity, or naturalized populations outside historic range
Policy implication: EW species can be 'de-listed' to CR upon successful reintroduction
Indian relevance: Saharan Cypress, Sophora toromiro — important for Prelims species questions
Distinction from CR: a CR species still has wild populations; EW has zero wild individuals

concepts.name: Critically Endangered (CR): Quantitative Thresholds
key_dimensions: Five criteria (A–E): Population reduction, restricted range, small population size, quantitative analysis (PVA), very small/restricted population
Criterion A: ≥90% population reduction over 10 years/3 generations for CR (vs. 70% for EN, 50% for VU)
Criterion B: Area of Occupancy (AOO) <10 km² OR Extent of Occurrence (EOO) <100 km² for CR
Indian CR species trap: Great Indian Bustard (CR), Snow Leopard (VU not CR) — species-category matching

concepts.name: Area of Occupancy (AOO) vs. Extent of Occurrence (EOO): A Definitional Trap
key_dimensions: EOO: Area within the outermost boundary connecting all known occurrences (convex hull) — larger measure
AOO: Actual area occupied by the species within the EOO — always ≤ EOO
Standard grid cell size for AOO: 2×2 km = 4 km² per cell (IUCN standard)
Why the distinction matters: A species can have large EOO but tiny AOO (fragmented habitat) — drives CR/EN/VU classification

concepts.name: Endangered (EN) vs. Vulnerable (VU): Threshold Comparisons
key_dimensions: Population reduction thresholds: EN ≥70% vs. VU ≥50% over 10 years/3 generations (Criterion A)
EOO thresholds: EN <5,000 km² vs. VU <20,000 km²; AOO: EN <500 km² vs. VU <2,000 km²
Probability of extinction: EN ≥20% within 20 years/5 generations; VU ≥10% within 100 years
UPSC trap species: Bengal Tiger (EN → delisted debates), Ganges River Dolphin (EN), Indian Elephant (EN not CR)

concepts.name: Data Deficient (DD): The Most Misunderstood Category
key_dimensions: DD does NOT mean the species is safe — it may be highly threatened but lacks data
DD is NOT a threatened category — cannot be used as a proxy for threat level
Difference from NE: DD = assessed but insufficient data; NE = not yet assessed at all
Policy implication: DD species can receive conservation priority — precautionary principle application

concepts.name: Near Threatened (NT) and Least Concern (LC): The 'Safe' Categories
key_dimensions: NT: Close to qualifying for VU or likely to qualify in near future — a watch-list status
LC: Widespread and abundant — does not meet criteria for NT, VU, EN, or CR
Common error: Assuming LC means no conservation concern — some LC species have declining trends
Indian examples: Snow Leopard was downlisted from EN to VU (2017); Nilgiri Tahr is EN — category changes are examinable

concepts.name: The Five Criteria (A–E) for Threatened Status Assessment
key_dimensions: Criterion A: Past/projected population decline (most commonly applied criterion)
Criterion B: Geographic range (EOO + AOO) with fragmentation/decline/fluctuation conditions
Criterion C: Small and declining population size (<2,500 mature individuals for EN)
Criterion D: Very small population (<250 mature individuals for EN) or very restricted AOO; Criterion E: Quantitative analysis (Population Viability Analysis)

concepts.name: Mature Individuals: The Key Population Metric
key_dimensions: IUCN uses 'mature individuals' not total population — excludes juveniles, dormant seeds in some cases
Why this matters: A species with 10,000 total individuals but only 200 mature → qualifies as EN under Criterion D
Implications for plants: Seed banks complicate mature individual counts
UPSC trap: Questions may give total population and ask category — must apply mature individual threshold

concepts.name: Generation Length: Its Role in Threshold Calculations
key_dimensions: Generation length = average age of parents in current population — NOT age at first reproduction
Longer generation = longer time window for Criterion A assessment (e.g., elephants: ~25 years → 75-year window)
Why large, slow-reproducing species are more vulnerable: fewer generations to recover
Contrast: Short generation species (insects) assessed over 10 years; long-lived species over 3 generations — whichever is longer

concepts.name: IUCN Red List vs. CITES Appendices: Overlap and Divergence
key_dimensions: IUCN Red List = conservation status assessment (non-binding); CITES = trade regulation treaty (legally binding)
A species can be LC on IUCN but listed on CITES Appendix I (e.g., trade threat despite stable population)
Reverse trap: CR species not listed on CITES if trade is not the primary threat
CITES Appendix I ≠ CR; Appendix II ≠ VU/EN — no automatic equivalence (common exam trap)

concepts.name: IUCN Red List vs. Wildlife Protection Act (WPA) 1972 Schedules
key_dimensions: WPA Schedules I–IV = Indian legal protection levels; IUCN categories = global assessment — different frameworks
A species can be Schedule I (highest Indian protection) but LC globally (e.g., Bengal Fox)
Conversely, a globally CR species may have weaker Schedule protection in India historically
2022 WPA Amendment reorganized schedules from 6 to 4 — examinees must know new structure vs. IUCN categories

concepts.name: Red List Index (RLI): Measuring Aggregate Biodiversity Change
key_dimensions: RLI tracks change in aggregate extinction risk across groups of species over time (0=all EX, 1=all LC)
Used as an SDG indicator: SDG 15.5.1 — Halting biodiversity loss measurement
Difference from the Red List itself: RLI is a trend indicator; Red List is a status snapshot
Limitation: Only valid for fully assessed taxonomic groups — birds and mammals most reliable

concepts.name: Regional vs. Global Red List Assessments
key_dimensions: A species can be Regionally CR but Globally LC if the regional population is a marginal fraction
IUCN guidelines require regional assessments to consider immigration from outside the region (rescue effect)
Indian context: Several species are regionally threatened in India but globally of lower concern
Policy trap: India's conservation decisions must reference both global IUCN status AND regional/national assessments

concepts.name: Downlisting and Uplisting: Conservation Success and Failure Stories
key_dimensions: Downlisting (improvement): Snow Leopard EN→VU (2017), Southern White Rhino recovery story
Uplisting (deterioration): African Elephant split into Forest Elephant (CR) and Savanna Elephant (EN) in 2021
Indian species status changes: Asiatic Lion (EN), Tiger population recovery — but global vs. subspecies status trap
Significance for UPSC: Recent re-assessments (last 3 years) are high-yield for Prelims current affairs

concepts.name: Flagship, Keystone, Umbrella, and Indicator Species: Overlap with Red List
key_dimensions: These ecological roles are independent of Red List status — an LC species can be a keystone species
UPSC frequently tests whether examinees conflate conservation priority (Red List) with ecological role
Tiger as umbrella species: protecting its habitat protects many other species — but its EN status is Red List, not umbrella status
Indicator species may be LC but signal ecosystem health — Red List CR status doesn't automatically make a species an indicator

concepts.name: High-Profile Indian Species and Their Correct IUCN Categories
key_dimensions: CR: Great Indian Bustard, Gharial, Pygmy Hog, Malabar Large-spotted Civet, Namdapha Flying Squirrel
EN: Indian Elephant, Ganges River Dolphin, Nilgiri Tahr, Lion-tailed Macaque, Dhole
VU: Snow Leopard, Gaur, Sloth Bear, Striped Hyena, Indian Giant Squirrel
Common traps: Bengal Tiger is EN (not CR); One-horned Rhino is VU (not EN); Asiatic Lion is EN (not CR)

concepts.name: Taxonomic Bias in Red List Assessments: Vertebrate-centric Coverage
key_dimensions: Nearly all birds and mammals assessed; <1% of insects formally assessed — creates knowledge gap
Plants: ~44,000 assessed out of estimated 390,000 species — majority unknown
Policy implication: Red List may underestimate true extinction crisis due to invertebrate/plant data gaps
DD category as a signal of taxonomic bias — many invertebrates default to DD or NE
